title: not a book
hook: not a book — a scroll, hand-written, read to the end and rolled back

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mezuzah, handwritten words on the doorpost. Your line was take the words with you. Did a doorway remind you? Day twenty.
screen: `THE MEZUZAH — TAKE THE WORDS WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Imagine a book that nobody is allowed to print. Every copy has to be written by hand, letter by letter, with a feather, on animal skin, by someone trained for years. One copy takes about a year. If a single letter is missing, or two letters touch, the whole thing can't be used until it's fixed. Nobody touches the writing with their fingers; they follow it with a silver pointer. When it's carried through a room, people stand, and some reach out to kiss it. When one is too old to use, it's buried like a person. Today: the scroll at the center of Jewish life.
screen: `A BOOK NOBODY CAN PRINT.` → `A YEAR TO WRITE ONE COPY.` → `CARRIED, KISSED, BURIED.`

segments.voice: Torah comes from a Hebrew root that means to aim, to point, to teach. Torah is teaching, instruction, the way pointed out. In its narrowest sense, it's the five books of Moses, Genesis to Deuteronomy, written in a scroll by a scribe called a sofer. Something over three hundred thousand letters, every one counted. Wider, Torah means the whole of the Hebrew Bible. Wider still, all of Jewish teaching, down to a good answer given at a kitchen table last night. The Psalms describe it, in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation, like this: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." Not a floodlight. A lamp, enough for the next step. Here's the part that makes it different from a book on a shelf. The scroll is read, in public, from beginning to end, one section each week, over a year. And on the autumn festival called Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah, the reader finishes the last lines of Deuteronomy, and immediately, without a pause, rolls the whole scroll back and starts again with Genesis. People dance with the scrolls in their arms. The story is never finished. There's a well-known teaching about the letters, too. The Torah ends with the letter lamed and begins with the letter bet. Put the end next to the beginning, and they spell lev, heart. The scroll runs in a circle, and the circle is a heart. So the Torah isn't a book you finish. It's a book a whole people reads together, at the same pace, year after year, for more than two thousand years.
screen: `TORAH — TEACHING, THE WAY POINTED OUT.` · `A LAMP, ENOUGH FOR THE NEXT STEP.` · `FINISHED, ROLLED BACK, BEGUN AGAIN.` · `LAMED AND BET SPELL HEART.` · then, large: `A LAMP UNTO MY FEET.`

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Think of one teaching that has lit the next step for you: a line from a parent, a teacher, a book, a text you love. Not a whole philosophy. One sentence. Say it to yourself slowly, like a scribe copying it one letter at a time. Then ask where it's pointing you next. The bell holds the time.
Torah. Teaching: a handwritten scroll, read from end back to beginning, year after year. Twentieth word.
Your line: the world's oldest book club. Today, share one line you love with someone else, the way a whole people shares one scroll. Day twenty.

howItsDone: In synagogue the Torah scroll is taken from the ark, carried through the congregation, and read aloud in a set portion each Sabbath, finishing and beginning again each year on Simchat Torah with singing and dancing.

original.note: Hebrew: teaching, instruction, from a root meaning to aim or point the way.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Jewish bible.
what it means: teaching. a handwritten scroll a whole people reads together, end back to beginning, every year.
what a scholar hears: the root y-r-h, to aim or shoot, gives moreh, teacher. the scroll ends with lamed and opens with bet: together, lev, heart.

notes: Letter count given loosely as 'over three hundred thousand' (commonly 304,805); confirm.
'About a year' for a scribe to write a scroll is typical but varies; confirm.
The lamed–bet 'lev' teaching is a popular homily; stated as 'a well-known teaching'. Confirm.
Burial of worn scrolls (geniza/burial) stated simply; confirm.
'More than two thousand years' of public reading is hedged; confirm.
